question: Marie Curie's laboratory notebooks from the 1890s are kept in a French national library, but anyone who wants to read them must sign a waiver and wear protective clothing, and the notebooks are stored in lead-lined boxes. Why?
alternative_answers: Radium has a very long half-life, so they stay radioactive
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Marie Curie's Belongings Will Be Radioactive For Another 1,500 Years

extra.verification_notes: Curie's notebooks at the BnF are kept in lead-lined boxes and remain radioactive from radium-226 contamination (half-life ~1,600 years), per https://www.sciencealert.com/these-personal-effects-of-marie-curie-will-be-radioactive-for-another-1-500-years.

explanation: Curie worked with radium and polonium without any shielding, so her notebooks, furniture and even her cookbook became contaminated with radium. Radium-226 has a half-life of around 1,600 years, which means the papers will remain radioactive for well over a thousand more years. The Bibliothèque nationale de France therefore stores them in lead-lined boxes and asks readers to accept the risk and wear protective gear before handling them.

question: A former textile worker and hobby parachutist, which cosmonaut became the first woman in space in 1963?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: a textile factory worker and an amateur skydiver

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the first woman in space was a trained pilot or scientist from the 1980s; she was a Soviet textile worker and amateur parachutist flying alone in 1963.
extra.verification_notes: Tereshkova, a former textile factory worker and amateur skydiver, became the first woman in space on Vostok 6 on 16 June 1963 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentina_Tereshkova).

explanation: She orbited Earth 48 times alone aboard Vostok 6, and to this day she is still the only woman ever to fly a solo space mission.

question: Which researcher, watching a chimpanzee strip leaves from a twig to fish for termites in 1960, became the first to document a wild animal making a tool?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: tool creation by non-human animals had never been observed. Until then, tool making was considered one of the defining characteristics of being human.

extra.why_interesting: Tool-making was treated as the defining human trait; one young woman with no degree watching a chimp named David Greybeard overturned that in a single observation.
extra.verification_notes: Goodall observed David Greybeard modifying twigs to fish for termites in Nov 1960, the first documented tool-making by a non-human animal; no later development contradicts this (https://wiki.janegoodall.org/wiki/Tool_Making).

explanation: Her mentor Louis Leakey replied that science must now redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as human.

question: Who remains the only person in history to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: She was and still is the only person to be awarded Nobel Prizes in two scientific categories.

extra.why_interesting: Players know she won a Nobel, but many do not realise that a record set over a century ago by a woman has never been matched by anyone since.
extra.verification_notes: Curie (Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911) is still the only person with Nobel Prizes in two different sciences; Pauling's second prize was Peace, per https://www.nobelprize.org/stories/women-who-changed-science/marie-curie/

explanation: She took Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911, and her daughter Irène later won a Nobel in Chemistry too, making them the only mother and daughter laureates.

question: Whose refusal to give up her seat on a city bus in Alabama in 1955 set off a boycott that lasted more than a year?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955, for refusing to surrender her seat to a white passenger.

extra.why_interesting: A single quiet act on an ordinary evening commute set off a protest that lasted more than a year and launched the civil rights movement.
extra.verification_notes: Parks' Dec 1, 1955 arrest triggered the Montgomery bus boycott, which ran until Dec 20, 1956; Colvin's earlier refusal did not trigger it.

explanation: The Montgomery boycott ran for 381 days and ended only when the US Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional.

question: Which 1940s Hollywood star co-patented a frequency-hopping radio system for guiding torpedoes, an idea that underpins today's Wi-Fi and Bluetooth?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Lamarr co-invented a radio guidance system for Allied torpedoes that used spread spectrum and frequency hopping technology

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a glamorous 1940s film star and a radio engineer as two different people; here they are the same woman, and her idea is in every phone.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Lamarr co-invented (with George Antheil) the frequency-hopping torpedo guidance system, US patent 2,292,387 (1942); the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth link is a slight simplification but is commonly accepted.

explanation: Lamarr worked out the scheme with avant-garde composer George Antheil, who suggested synchronising the hops the way a player piano syncs its rolls.

question: The US Department of Defense named its standard programming language after which 19th-century woman, often called the first computer programmer?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: named after Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace, usually known as Ada Lovelace

extra.why_interesting: Players know a Victorian countess is called the first programmer, but few connect her to a modern military language whose standard number is literally her birth year.
extra.verification_notes: Ada was developed under DoD contract and named after Ada Lovelace; the 1997 end of the mandate doesn't affect the past-tense 'named' claim (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_(programming_language)).

explanation: The language is simply called Ada, and the Pentagon gave its 1980 standard the number 1815, the year she was born.

question: Which future prime minister studied chemistry at Oxford under Dorothy Hodgkin, the Nobel laureate who worked out the structure of penicillin and vitamin B12?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Following her arrival at Oxford, Roberts began studies under X-ray crystallographer Dorothy Hodgkin, the tutor in chemistry for Somerville College since 1934.

extra.why_interesting: Players file prime ministers under law or politics, not laboratories; the Iron Lady was a research chemist trained by a Nobel laureate.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Thatcher (then Roberts) studied chemistry at Oxford under Dorothy Hodgkin, who supervised her thesis.

explanation: Thatcher worked as a research chemist before entering politics and kept a portrait of Hodgkin hanging in 10 Downing Street.

question: Before orbiting Earth in 1962, John Glenn refused to fly until which NASA mathematician had re-checked the computer's trajectory figures by hand?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Glenn had asked for her specifically and had refused to fly unless Johnson verified the calculations.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume NASA trusted its machines; the first American to orbit Earth trusted one woman's pencil arithmetic more than the computer.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Glenn refused to fly until Katherine Johnson verified the computer's calculations; no newer event affects this.

explanation: Her story was later told in the film Hidden Figures, and she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom at the age of 97.

question: True or false: Indira Gandhi, India's first female prime minister, was the daughter of Mahatma Gandhi.
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Her father, Jawaharlal Nehru, was a leading figure in the Indian movement for independence from British rule

extra.why_interesting: The shared surname makes nearly everyone assume a family link to the Mahatma; the real political dynasty is the Nehru family.
extra.verification_notes: Indira Gandhi's father was Jawaharlal Nehru, not Mahatma Gandhi, so the statement is false and the claimed answer 'False' is correct.

explanation: Her father was Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, and the Gandhi name came from her husband Feroze, who was no relation to the Mahatma.

question: Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in 1431. In which year did the Catholic Church finally declare her a saint?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Canonized: 16 May 1920 by Pope Benedict XV

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a medieval martyr became a saint in the medieval era; it took the Church nearly five centuries, and the ceremony happened after the First World War.
extra.verification_notes: Joan of Arc was canonized on 16 May 1920 by Pope Benedict XV, per Wikipedia; 1456 was the rehabilitation trial, not canonization.

explanation: A retrial cleared her name in 1456, but sainthood only came in 1920, a few years after soldiers had carried her image through the trenches of the First World War.

question: Three of these scientists won a Nobel Prize. Which one never did?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Francis Crick, James Watson, and Maurice Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962

extra.why_interesting: All four are celebrated women scientists whose names sit side by side in textbooks; only someone who knows the Nobel history can spot the one who was never honoured.
extra.verification_notes: Curie, Hodgkin and McClintock are Nobel laureates; Franklin died in 1958 and never won (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalind_Franklin).

explanation: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images were key to the structure of DNA, but she died in 1958 and the Nobel for that discovery went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins four years later.

question: Apart from the Curies, only one woman has a chemical element named in her honour. Which physicist, who first explained nuclear fission, is it?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Unbinilium and Ubn are the temporary systematic IUPAC name and symbol respectively, which are used until the element is discovered, confirmed, and a permanent name is decided upon.

extra.why_interesting: Players know Curie has an element; they rarely know that the only other woman on the periodic table is the physicist who explained nuclear fission and was passed over for the Nobel.
extra.verification_notes: Meitnerium (element 109) honours Lise Meitner, and no new element has been named for a woman since; element 120 remains undiscovered per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium.

explanation: Element 109 is meitnerium, a belated tribute to the woman whose collaborator Otto Hahn alone received the Nobel Prize for the discovery of fission.

question: In 1960, which island nation became the first country in the world to be led by a female prime minister?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: the first woman in the world to be democratically elected prime minister in 1960.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Britain, Israel or India as the first country with a woman head of government; the real answer is a small island nation, years before any of them.
extra.verification_notes: Sirimavo Bandaranaike became PM of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) in July 1960, the world's first female head of government; the 1960 name was Ceylon but Sri Lanka is the same country (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirimavo_Bandaranaike).

explanation: Sirimavo Bandaranaike took office in what was then called Ceylon, nine years before Golda Meir and almost two decades before Margaret Thatcher.

question: As a Cambridge PhD student in 1967, who noticed the regular radio pulses, jokingly nicknamed Little Green Men, that turned out to be the first known pulsar?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: The signal was temporarily dubbed 'Little Green Man 1' (LGM-1) before the source, now designated PSR B1919+21, was identified as a rapidly rotating neutron star.

extra.why_interesting: The signal was so regular the team half-joked about aliens; the student who found it in kilometres of chart paper was left out when the Nobel came.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Bell Burnell, as a Cambridge PhD student, detected the first pulsar signal in 1967 (LGM-1); no later events invalidate this.

explanation: The 1974 Nobel Prize for the discovery went to her supervisor Antony Hewish instead, a decision still cited as one of the great Nobel snubs.
